speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour, of which I gave him notice yesterday. What consideration, if any, is the government giving to the suggestion to the unemployed that they would be
[Mr. Hans ell.)

well advised to remain in the community in which they now live unless directed to some other labour field in the Canadian market by the officers of the unemployment insurance commission?

subtopic: SUGGESTED INSTRUCTIONS TO UNEMPLOYED
speechtext:
appreciate the hon. member's courtesy in giving me notice of this question. The question naturally divides itself into two parts. In the first place the government, or the unemployment insurance commission in this case, is hardly in a position to suggest to an individual who is interested in finding work that he should remain in a locality where he cannot get employment. People will insist on remaining free to look for work wherever it may be found. As long as they succeed in finding it, this is a good principle and one with which there should be no interference.
In the second place, Mr. Speaker, when it becomes evident that work is simply not to be had in a certain locality, that activity has dried up and there is little likelihood of work being found, or where the supply of workers is far in excess of the available jobs and will likely remain so, then the Department of Labour has recommended that such areas be declared labour surplus areas and transportation assistance has been supplied to workers who have promises of jobs in other regions. Windsor, Ontario; Spring-hill and New Glasgow, Nova Scotia; and St. Stephen, New Brunswick, have been declared such areas. In a few days Tilbury, Ontario, will be declared a labour surplus area.

speechtext:
would like to refer, Mr. Speaker, to a question which was asked of me yesterday by the

hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Macdonald). The question was whether I would make available a report of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police dealing with charges of bribery and conspiracy in the granting of forest management licences in the province of British Columbia. I made a partial answer yesterday, and I undertook to check up on the circumstances surrounding this situation.
I am now able to advise the house that this case was investigated by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at the request of the attorney general of the province of British Columbia and as a function called for under the contract between the government of Canada and the government of the province of British Columbia for the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The investigation, as I tentatively indicated yesterday, was therefore an entirely provincial matter, and the report is not one which I am at liberty to disclose.
I may say in addition, Mr. Speaker, that the work carried out by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in British Columbia under the policing agreement is paid for at rates set down in the agreement and based upon a division of the per capita operating costs of the force. Charges to the provinces are therefore not apportioned in any way to individual cases such as this.
Mr. Speaker, I was particularly concerned to establish in my own mind, and because several hon. members are interested in this matter, whether I would have any authority to disclose the report. In the course of investigation I checked what I believed to be the relevant clause of the agreement then in force between the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia under which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police carry on provincial policing. The relevant clause of the agreement then in force, clause 2, recites that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police shall perform the duties of the former British Columbia provincial police force:
*-in accordance with the wishes and under the direction of the attorney general of the province of British Columbia in the same manner and to the same extent as if the British Columbia provincial police were still in existence.
It therefore appears to be clear that the question of whether or not the report is to be made public is a matter entirely within the authority of the provincial attorney general.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I refer to a question put to me on October 23 by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort, which is to be found at page 317 of Hansard and is in these words:
Is the minister aware that when a farmer makes application for a loan from the Canadian farm loan hoard the board, before acknowledging the request, informs implement companies in the area of the application and of the board's disposition of the request for the loan? If the minister finds this to be the case, would he assure the house that he will instruct the hoard to cease immediately this unethical, high-handed and deplorable practice?
I have made inquiries, and have made them in the spirit that I indicated in my reply in the house at that time. I am assured there is no practice on the part of the Canadian farm loan board such as the hon. member implied in his question. I am told that in many cases when an application is received it is necessary to check on the statement of liabilities submitted by the applicant, this being a natural procedure in testing the propriety of granting the loan.
Of course these inquiries concerning credit oftentimes require checking, and apart from information concerning the amount of large claims, it is sometimes necessary to seek other confidential information from other business concerns such as banks, implement companies and retail credit reporting organizations. To do this it is often necessary to furnish some information.
I am assured that the staff of the board are very conscious of the necessity of treating any information of this nature, whether given or received, in a strictly confidential manner, and am further assured that the

Inquiries of the Ministry board's general practices, ethics and attitude in this regard compare favourably with those of others in a similar position.
My hon. friend's question arose out of a particular case. He was good enough to send me a copy of a letter involved in that case. I do not think it is necessary that I go beyond the answer to my friend's general question and refer to the circumstances of that particular case. But at the worst what happened in that case evidently was a breach of confidence on the part of a certain person, I believe not connected with the board. However, if my hon. friend is interested I shall be glad to show him the correspondence in this matter, for I have made it my business to inquire into it thoroughly and I can assure my hon. friend and the house that no such practice as his question implied would be tolerated for a moment.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, October 30, consideration in committee of Bill No. 14, to provide for advance payments for prairie grain prior to delivery thereof- Mr. Harkness (for Mr. Churchill)-Mr. Courtemanche in the chair.
On clause 10-Lien on grain.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this clause, Mr. Chairman. Since I am from a rural riding in Ontario, I was pleased to see the government notice of motion with regard to a measure concerning general agricultural products on today's order paper.
It seems to me that under this particular bill, when a producer applies for an advance

Grain
on a certain number of bushels he is in fact selling a number of bushels of grain to the board. Since the board cannot accept the grain he is offering to sell he has to store it in his own storage place. He no longer owns the grain but is holding it for the board. I believe that somewhere in the bill it should be made clear that the producer is actually holding this grain in trust for the board. The minister may feel that the bill is sufficiently clear, but I do feel that the position of trust in which the producer is placed should be clearly stated.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last night
before we adjourned I listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion that was taking place on this particular clause. I listened to some of the objections which were made from this part of the chamber, and I listened with interest to the minister's replies. What I have to say now does not call for any particular elaboration of the minister's reply, but it does appear to me now that the bill is not quite as rosy as it first appeared to be.
When the resolution was first introduced and some publicity was given to the measure across the country, the impression was left that the wheat farmer was now going to receive some spending money. He thought he would be able to buy a few new things; that he would not be quite so hard up now as he might have been had the advance payment idea not been brought forward.
I believe it is obvious to all, Mr. Chairman, that there are two classes of farmers so far as this particular piece of legislation is concerned. There are those who are well enough off that they will not have to take advantage of this legislation. I do not know how many farmers of this type exist, perhaps not very many, but there are some who are sufficiently well off that they do not have to take advantage of it.
The other class of farmer is the farmer who has not any money, the small farmer, the farmer who is hard up and has been hard up. If this bill was intended to furnish some ready cash to the farmer who is hard up, it does not meet the situation. It does not meet the situation by reason of the fact that if there are any liens against the farmer's wheat, which certainly would apply to those farmers who are hard up because they are the ones who have had to go to the banks and borrow in the past or perhaps incur some other financial obligation, by reason of this clause the bill will aid the creditors and not the farmers who need the money.
I know, of course, the minister's argument. So long as these liens exist and this legislation does not by-pass those liens, the farmer who is hard up is better off in so far as he
will be able to get 50 cents a bushel for his wheat to help pay off his debts.
That does not give him any ready cash just the same. I want to make that observation because I am afraid that now the bill is falling far short of what the farmers expected and of the impression that may have been left during the election campaign when the speakers on behalf of the Conservative party were so anxious to get into office and made the promise that they were going to take care of the poor farmer.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
In reply to the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, I would just say that this bill does not fall short in any respect of what most of the farmers expected and what they were led to expect. This bill, of course, does not provide cash, as has been pointed out several times in this debate, for the man who has no grain, such as the man who was hailed out or flooded out or who for any other cause did not produce any grain. This bill does not help him because he has not any grain on which to make an advance.
But as to a farmer who has a considerable number of debts to the people to whom he owes them-whether it is the municipality, the men who threshed his grain or the hail insurance board which gave him hail insurance, any liens along that line

naturally the bill cannot be of such a nature that it will cut those people out of their right to secure part of that farmer's grain in order to discharge their claims. I hope that no hon. member in this house is trying to maintain that we should bring in legislation which would make null and void the ordinary civil rights which farmers and others have in their respective provinces and that their creditors have against them in those provinces.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened carefully to what the minister has said just now and I also have in mind the fact that this legislation is supposed to meet an emergency. However, in emergencies you do not take the line which the minister has just taken. In my opinion, nobody is better qualified than is the farmer himself, to say just what he should do with the money. Individual cases vary. He himself is best informed as to where that money should go.
Here is the main difference between this piece of legislation and that which was put on the statute books the year before last by the previous administration and which was criticized by the present government as a loans act because it contained an interest clause. In that particular legislation interest was provided for; under this legislation the money is interest free. But in the previous

Grain
legislation one thing was determined for sure, that was that the money would definitely go to the farmer, that it would get into his hands and that he himself would decide where it would go. This is not a loans to farmers act or an assistance to farmers act or an advance to farmers act whatever. It is a cash advances to farmers creditors act or a farmers creditors assistance act. The farmer is the last man who is considered here. Anybody can put in a lien against the farmer with the elevator company-and the municipalities will certainly do so-with the result that the farmer will get what is left after everybody else gets through with it. This is not the kind of legislation that is going to do any particular good in the west.
I have had experience in doing business in western Canada and have done business with farmers on a credit basis many times. Many of them still owe me money. If I wanted to take advantage of this act I could put liens against prospective borrowers under this scheme. This is not the answer to the problem of putting cash in farmers' hands. This piece of legislation has been built up with a great deal of ballyhoo and window dressing. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources tells us that this legislation may put $186 million in the hands of western farmers; it will do no such thing. In fact, it will be rather hard to decide just what money this legislation actually will put in the hands of the farmers by the time these creditors get through reckoning up what they want.
I think the government had perhaps better bring in an amendment to this part of the bill and change it to make sure that this money gets into the farmers' hands if they are concerned for the farmers in the west. In this debate they have said that they know the farmers are honest. I think the first concern of any farmer is not only just to pay his bills but to keep his family alive. With the type of crops that some of them have had this fall, where either through drought or through conditions which prevailed through the northern part of the province where they have had seven weeks' or eight weeks' of rain in a row, their crops are completely deteriorated and they are in difficulty. If they can get this money it should be put in their hands and they themselves should decide what they should do with it. There should not be built into this legislation the provision that everybody else gets his first and the farmer gets his last.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the statements that have just been made should be answered. The total amounts that

were secured by the farmers in western Canada during the two years that the interim financing act was in effect were, in one year, $8 million and, in the other year, $4 million. That was the total amount in those two years. The smallness arose from the fact that the farmer was obliged to pay interest. My hon. friend now says that this act will not be effectual because of the fact that amounts which are owing to creditors would naturally be subject to payment. All I can say in that regard is that there is in the federal parliament no power in any way to disallow liens and their effectuality, for liens and other charges are matters under provincial jurisdiction. It is a strange attitude that my hon. friend takes. He votes for the legislation but he says it is not going to be effectual. He points out that last year and two years ago the loan legislation was effectual. To me the position which he takes is not understandable in view of the figures, $8 million in one year and $4 million in the other.
This legislation before the house today is the legislation in effect that is asked for by the farm organizations in western Canada. I am not going to read them but I have before me the recommendations made by the western farm organizations and in particular the one in Saskatoon in October, 1955 which asked for cash advances. The position taken by my hon. friend is a strange one. My friend the hon. member for Melville left the impression that if the former government had come into power this legislation providing for cash advances would in fact have been introduced. At least, that was my understanding of what he stated the other day. My friend the hon. member for Meadow Lake says that a claim such as he would have as an oil dealer would be another charge. That is not so. The only possibility of any creditor having a charge as against the credit of any farmer in western Canada would be either under a writ of execution or under a bill of sale or a chattel mortgage given at some time during the year. As to the bill of sale, it would only be effectual if it was actually entered into after the harvesting began and the cutting had been done.
From my interpretation of the attitude of the western farmer, as expressed since this legislation was brought in, there is general appreciation of the fact that this government acted, whereas in the past two or three years in the face of almost universal demand for action in this regard in western Canada the members of the previous government, for reasons known to themselves, did not act. As a matter of fact one of the excuses given for not acting was that given in 1955 by the hon. member for Rosthern. He made several speeches in this house in this regard in 1955.

His contention was that if cash advances were introduced they would destroy the wheat board and that this general demand for cash advances would interfere with the operation of the wheat board and would in fact constitute its destruction.
The other day he said we did not go far enough, we only went half as far as we should have gone. I do not understand that inconsistency. 1 believe this legislation, as far as it is practicable within our constitutional limitations, is the uttermost step that could be taken in order to provide the western farmer with an advance on wheat which is as yet unmarketed in consequence of and for reasons which I am not going to go into at this time. Suffice it to say that when my hon. friend states that because he has an oil agency he thereby would be able to interfere, or because somebody owed him for gasoline he would therefore be able to secure any portion of this advance, it is as unwarranted as it is incorrect.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Since I rose on this point yesterday I think I should say a few things in regard to the statements which have just been made, particularly the reference to what I said on an earlier occasion. I did state in the earlier stages of the discussion that representations had been made last spring by the farm organizations in western Canada to the outgoing government to the effect that they desired to have something done along this line and the decision was then reached that the matter would be further discussed in the autumn. It was stated at that time, I believe, that if the bill which was brought down was in the same form as we had reason to believe last spring it would be, it would naturally be a measure which we would be inclined to support. Even in its present form I would be inclined to say we would support it but I would like to point out to my hon. friend that the argument he has just used is the argument used with regard to the act which did provide for bank loans and if he has not had any complaints from the farm organizations I cannot understand it, because the system set up under the act which was brought in was not in effect for one week before all the farm organizations of western Canada raised a terrific row about the very point he is discussing.
I may say that there is pinned on the wall in every elevator in Saskatchewan, so that everybody who takes in a load of grain can see it, a file of liens against the grain so delivered and right at the top of that list will be the lien for unpaid taxes. This is in accordance with the provincial law. The same kind of argument with regard to provincial 96698-39
Grain
authorities and collections and so on was raised when the plan based on the bank loan legislation was being set up.
I happened to be out at my farm at that time and the solicitor for the wheat pool phoned me and asked me if we considered that kind of legislation was going to provide cash for the farmers, because with the possibility of liens being effective the farmers would get very little of it.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Who was that solicitor?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Milligan. He asked for a meeting to be called for the purpose of discussing the whole issue and a meeting was called in the city of Winnipeg. The finance people also contacted me and the whole matter was reconsidered and ways and means found of doing away with having these taxes and other liens charged up against the loan. Under the bank loans arrangement, as stated by the member for Meadow Lake, when a man went to the bank to get a loan, if the banker attempted to take any money out of such loan to pay anyone he had no government guarantee at all. Therefore loans made under that arrangement meant that they could not charge anything against them. The banker could not take anything out; the municipality could not take anything out; no one could take anything out.
There would not be more than six or eight hundred dollars involved per person in most cases; some would run higher, but very few. Hon. members in this house who come from the west know that a half section or three-quarter section farmer often owes $450 in taxes or even more and if when he goes into the elevator to deliver his grain or to get his advance, or if when he goes to the bank to get cash the first thing that is done is to take that money out that farmer is not going to be in a position, of his own choice, to pay. The condition with respect to collection in this bill is the same as the other one was prior to change.
When a man drives to the elevator with a load, let us say of 150 bushels of grain, the proceeds from 75 bushels will be charged up to pay off the advance and the proceeds from 75 bushels will be handed to the farmer. No lien can be charged up against that in the sense that a lien was charged before while that transaction is being handled, but under this legislation it can be charged up. I do not think we should put through a bill in this house under a misunderstanding. If the government desires to put it through that way it only adds to the strength of the argument which I have made all the way through these discussions, that the limitations in this bill are greater than they were in the other one.

Grain
While my hon. friends are always saying that the amount of money available under this bill is so and so, that is the same argument as was used when we were dealing with the other bill; the money available is so and so but everyone in this house said "What is available is not going to be asked for". If the conditions put in the bill are such that the average farmer looks it over and sees the conditions under which he can get the advance are not satisfactory to him he is not going to go any further. I say there are already too many of those provisions in this bill.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I am in complete agreement, Mr. Chairman, with what has been said by the hon. member for Melville.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: In response to what the member for Melville and the member for Meadow Lake have said, to the effect that this bill is not as good as the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act which the previous government put through, and that there are more limitations in this than there were in the previous loan legislation, all their arguments in this connection really amount to nothing for the simple reason that the previous legislation is still on the statute books and is going to remain there. This bill does not do away with it and it is still there for the farmer who wishes to make use of the interim financing act rather than this cash advance act. He is at perfect liberty to choose. Therefore I cannot understand what these two members are talking about when they attempt to maintain that the loan legislation of the previous government was better than this proposed legislation and therefore the farmers would have been better off if the old system had been continued. That legislation is still continuing and is there for the farmer to take advantage of if he wishes to do so.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: But that legislation does not provide automatically for doing this. That legislation provides that the government has got to take certain action before it does it. The fact that the legislation is on the statute books does not settle all that.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the legislation is in effect at the present time.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: That is the point.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: Yes, it is in effect up to a certain time. Further action is required to keep it there.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
The Minister of Agriculture has referred to the fact that both these pieces of legislation are in effect; there is no argument about that.

That does not change the fact, and I say this with all due deference to the Prime Minister-because we have a lot of other things in common even though we do not share the same political faith-that in my opinion in giving his reply to what I said a few moments ago he walked all around the point I made and concluded by suggesting that, well, we will leave it up to the farmers. As I understood him, it is a matter of the jurisdiction of this parliament as to whether the suggestion I made that the money should go direct to the farmers could be made effective. He said we have no jurisdiction to do it and that is why it was not done.
I point out to him that, under the legislation just referred to by the Minister of Agriculture, this was done last year and the year before by this very legislation. It was made effective under that and that money did go into the hands of the farmer and no one could get their hands on any of it until the farmer got it in his hands and decided himself what he should do with it. That is the criticism I have of the present legislation. Irrespective of whether the bank loan legislation remains in effect, the present legislation has been built up before the public gaze as something that will do wonders in the west. That is the kind of window dressing it has been given. It is certainly not going to do wonders if it is not going to get cash into the hands of the farmer because he is the man we are concerned with in this legislation which was designed for the purpose of meeting the emergency situation that exists in the agricultural industry by putting money in the hands of the farmer.
If it is to go to other people, as was suggested by the hon. member for Melville, and if there are lists already on the walls of the local elevators outlining who has liens on the money-particularly municipalities-this legislation is not what it appears to be at all. This is not money for farmers but rather for farmers' creditors.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been very interested in the last few days in hearing the arguments brought forward by our friends across the way in opposition to this legislation the government is seeking to implement at the earliest possible moment in order that the wheat board can get the money into the hands of the farmers. We have listened to a lot of speeches which would have been more properly made on the debate in reply to the speech from the throne and could very well have been left until after the legislation has been put through. I know that the farmers in my area are anxious that this legislation be put into effect at the earliest possible time and I would like to

Grain
make some remarks with regard to a few of the comments made by hon. members across the way.
Several hon. gentlemen rose to say how much better the legislation brought in by the former government is as compared to the legislation before us. I would venture to say that the amount of money borrowed in the past under the bank loans legislation will show hon. members how ineffectual it was as compared to what will be accomplished by the present legislation. Under the bank loans legislation $7 million was spread over the prairie provinces.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: $13 million!

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
As a matter of fact the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act was supposed to make available to a farmer a loan of $3,000 but the experience was that when he went to borrow that sum he could not get it unless he was worth a great deal more than that sum. The result was that a great number of farmers did not take advantage of the act and they stayed away from it in droves. In effect it was a loan on the farmer's net worth.
It was suggested by the hon. member for Melville the other day that more money would be loaned under the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act than will be the case under the existing legislation and in reply to the hon. member I would say to let us wait and see the result.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: That is what I suggested.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
That is a good idea because I do not know of a farmer in Manitoba who would not take advantage of cash advances. Under this legislation the farmer is not given a loan but rather an advance on his grain just as if he had delivered it to the elevator.
As far as having the grain attached for arrears of municipal taxes is concerned, that is unheard of in Manitoba. I thought that under the governments you have in Saskatchewan and Alberta the municipalities would not be able to attach the farmer's grain. If he cannot pay his taxes it works a hardship on him but nothing should be done to take away his livelihood. We do not attach anyone's grain in Manitoba for arrears of taxes.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: You do not grow very much wheat, either, in Manitoba.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I will tell you we grow quite a bit of wheat and it is of good quality.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: About as much as they grow in Ontario and Quebec.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext: I was glad to hear the Prime Minister's explanation concerning liens today because I was not able to receive one from the Minister of Agriculture yesterday and I am pleased to learn that provincial, threshers' and municipal liens will take precedence over federal liens. However, there is one question I would like to ask. If there are liens against a farmer's grain will the federal government advance cash to him if his grain is already covered by a lien from some other source?

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I explained yesterday this is an advance and not a loan and therefore what applies to one does not apply to the other. When the advance is made it is just an advance payment for grain which is going to be delivered under the farmer's quota during the course of the crop year and every charge which would normally be collected against that

Grain
grain under provincial law naturally has to be taken into account as far as the advance is concerned.
All of this argument which has been going on here this afternoon on the part of various opposition members, and which was going on before the house closed yesterday afternoon, really amounts to an argument that there is no use in a farmer delivering his grain at all if he has any debts. That is the logical end of that argument and it is really what the argument amounts to; that if a farmer has debts there is no use in his delivering his grain. If you are going to take that position, then I think you had better say that any farmer who has debts had better go out of business and forget the whole thing.
What does the farmer want to deliver his grain for? Why in many cases does he want the advance if not to discharge some of those debts which make it impossible for him to carry on in a reasonable manner? In most instances that is the very reason why he wants to get the advance. It is to pay the storekeeper, the threshing bill, his taxes, and so on. As far as the argument is concerned that he is not going to get enough cash to do this, which was put up by the hon. member for Melville, or the hon. member for Meadow Lake, one or the other as I pointed *out on second reading of the bill, the farmer who has only 50 specified acres will still get as cash in hand under this scheme, if he had No. 1 northern we will say, about $370 from his unit quota, the initial amount that he could deliver, and then he is eligible . for a further advance of $150. Now, that is the man who has only 50 specified acres and, of course, it goes up from there.
In other words, this is a scheme which is designed to put a reasonable amount of cash in a farmer's hands, even though he is not able to deliver any grain beyond the unit quota which, of course, he has done in most instances already. It is a scheme which is specifically designed to help the small farmer. In these circumstances, all these extraneous arguments which have been raised in regard to farmers who have debts I do not think really are applicable and certainly in that regard, I repeat, it is an argument that a farmer who has debts might just as well not deliver his grain at all.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 11 and 12 agreed to.
On clause 13-Default.

maintopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE CASH ADVANCES ON FARM-STORED GRAIN
speechtext:
This is the clause which defines the various instances in which a producer, having taken' a cash advance, may be in
[Mr. Harkness.l
default. Subclause (a) says that he may be in default within 10 days after the date on which the board mails or delivers or causes to be mailed or delivered a notice stating that he should pay his advance.
A second instance in which a man may be in default is that of a producer who has not applied for a permit book before the 15th day of September. That, of course, means that on that evidence itself the farmer is no longer in business. That would be the reasoning and I have no objection to it. But subclause (c) says that a producer may be in default if:
Before the 31st day of December In the new crop year immediately following the crop year in which the advance payment was made, or such later date as the board may authorize in special cases.
That is to say, if the producer has not paid his advance by December 31, apart from whatever special cases may be allowed, he is automatically in default. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the minister should move for the deletion of subparagraph (c). It seems to me that a man in default is adequately defined to meet every instance, apart from this. The only time in which a man would be in default under this subparagraph, or the most frequent time, is if he has not had an opportunity to deliver his grain against the advance which has been made. I am sure the minister will not say that this is not a situation that is likely to arise, because the conditions that would arise under this situation are likely to be quite prevalent on December 31, since today about three-quarters of the marketing points in western Canada are on a unit quota, which means they are not under a quota at all so far as this legislation is concerned.
Therefore, with the clause in the bill as it now stands, if a producer on December 31, for example, has had an opportunity to deliver only four bushels of grain, because the quota and space were not available, and if you get on into December when the unit quota is still in existence and there is no standard quota, unless there is a big change in the grain situation it is quite probable that thousands of producers will be automatically in default under this subclause on December 31, through no fault of their own.

We have had quite a long talk from the Minister of Agriculture who was piloting this bill through for the Minister of Trade and Commerce regarding the fact that he thought the farmers were fairly honest. I am not disputing that. I also think the farmers are honest. Give them an opportunity and they will pay their obligations when they can do so.
This clause has nothing whatever to do with any loan that any other creditor may have, so far as this bill is concerned, except that which the federal government has as a guarantor for the loans made by the banks. I went to some length yesterday in arguing the case; I do not intend to go over that ground again but I do think it is possible that under this clause those farmers who have found themselves in great need and have had to borrow money under the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act, 1956, will find themselves in the position where they are going to be required to pay off those liens before they can get any cash whatever from those cash advances. It may happen that they will not get one cent of the cash advance to use for the purpose, as we were told, for which this legislation was intended.
Certainly if this clause means anything at all it means that the farmers who are in great need of cash to pay those small bills which they have been running up over the last few months through no fault of their own will not be able to get it for that purpose. They must have some cash in order to pay their obligations to the local grocery man, or to the local man who has been supplying them with fuel oil for harvesting purposes, or to the butcher. These bills were all run up on the assurance that the farmer would pay them out of the first moneys he got from the disposal of his grain. This bill does not propose to allow the farmer to sell his grain and get the initial payment. It only proposes that he shall get as high as 50 cents a bushel in advance.
It seems to me that the government has not got the same argument under this clause as it had under clause 10 in connection with which the Minister of Agriculture said that the government should not be a party to any legislation which would cause creditors to be put in the position where they could not get the money which was owing to them. He went on to point out that if the farmer owed [The Deputy Chairman.]
taxes he should pay those taxes and if there were other liens by the province he should pay those liens.
Surely that puts the farmer in the position of appearing to be dishonest. Irrespective of whether or not this clause stands, if the farmer sells his grain and gets the full 50 cents he is an honest man. I am sure that 99 per cent of the farmers of western Canada are honest, and the farmer does not need the federal government to tell him what to do with the money. If he has certain obligations he is going to take the money and pay his bills that of necessity he has been running up over the last few months. He will use the money to pay the bills of his creditors such as the grocery store or implement man or perhaps use part of it to buy some needed clothing for the children. He is not dishonest and he is not trying to avoid paying his just debts.
But in this clause the government says to the farmer that the very first claim is that of the government. They say to him that out of this 50 cents which was supposed to be so urgently needed he must pay any debt which is owing under the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act. It does not seem to me that the government will suffer if it waives this clause because it will still have a claim on any other grain that will be produced. The government will have a claim on any grain that the farmer brings in before he gets his full initial payment.
There is no possible chance of the farmer getting out from under his obligation to pay the loan which he obtained under the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act. The government is fully guaranteed and does not need this clause at all. If the government is going to be bullheaded-maybe that is not the right word but it expresses my feeling- and say, "No sir, we are going to demand our pound of flesh", then I say the government should be at least a little bit charitable and provide that the farmer will at least get 25 cents a bushel for his wheat.

The house resumed, from Friday, October 25, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Monteith

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Old Age Security Act to increase the amount of monthly pension payable thereunder to fifty-five dollars per month, to reduce the basic residence requirements for pensioners from twenty years to ten years and to increase the length of permissible temporary absences of pensioners from Canada from three to six months.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE AND RESIDENCE QUALIFICATIONS
speechtext:
When the minister introduced this resolution last Thursday, he explained that it had three objects. First of all, it would increase the amount of benefit to $55 per month; second, reduce the basic residence requirement from 20 years to 10; and, third extend the length of time which pensioners are free to spend outside of Canada in any year without loss of pension.
Then, he went on to make the following comment, as recorded at page 385 of Hansard for October 24, 1957:
In recommending these changes to the house the government is acting promptly to honour the pledges which our leader and our party made to the senior citizens of this country during the recent election.

As I do not share the opinion of the minister with regard to the honouring of the pledges which his leader and the party made during the recent election, I should like to take this occasion to review the promises that were made by the leader of the Conservative party and to examine the extent to which this resolution now before the committee implements those promises. The Prime Minister appears to have dealt with this subject of old age security when he opened the Conservative campaign in Toronto on April 25. According to the Toronto Star's report of the meeting, he promised:
Old age pensions would be set at a figure high enough to meet the needs of our older citizens and would be adjusted from time to time in accordance with changes in living costs. Similar consideration would be given war veterans and retired civil servants.
According to a Canadian Press report of the same meeting, the present Prime Minister said that:
A Conservative government would set payments high enough to meet the needs of the recipients, with subsequent adjustments to living costs and increases in national productivity.
Or in the words of the Globe and Mail which I do not think would be unsympathetic to the government in its account of the meeting:
Social security benefits would be geared to keep pace with Canada's productivity.
I therefore want to emphasize, Mr. Chairman, the fact that there were three points in this promise. First, the payments would be high enough to meet the needs of the recipients. Second, the payments would be adjusted from time to time to keep pace with increases in the cost of living. Third, the payments would be geared to national productivity. I should like to deal with each of these three points a little bit more fully.
As it is the government which has now fixed the payment to be made at $55 a month, and as the minister himself has said that this measure honoured the pledges which his party made, I think we are entitled to infer that the government considers that a sum of $55 per month meets the needs of our senior citizens. I hope, however, that this determination by the present government will not serve as a pretext for provincial governments to adopt the attitude that the setting of old age security at this amount of $55 a month relieves them of their constitutional responsibility for the care of the recipients, that is to say persons over 70 years of age who are unable to live on old age security alone.
I feel that this point is overlooked by many provincial governments which seem to believe that the institution of old age security
Old Age Security Act
on a universal basis has relieved them of the responsibility of caring for citizens who have attained or passed the age of 70 years and who are in need.
The second point of the Prime Minister's promise was that the payments of old age security would be adjusted from time to time to meet increases in the cost of living. As I pointed out earlier, that was a part of the promise made in Toronto on April 25. It was repeated again at Espanola, Ontario and again in Victoria, B.C. on May 21. Let me quote the words of the Prime Minister as reported in the Vancouver Province of May 22. These are his words:
I say to the old age pensioner, to the war veteran, to the retired civil service pensioner, we will provide lair and realistic pensions based on the cost of living and a fair comfort in living.
Though it is perfectly clear from the press accounts of the three meetings that I have just mentioned-Toronto, Espanola and Victoria-that this was an integral part of the Conservative pledge with respect to old age security, I want to add to the record the words the Prime Minister used in a broadcast on May 22, 1957. He said:
We intend, this September, to call together parliament and there and then fix a fair and reasonable amount for the old age pensioner, indeed for the other pensioners, and also make provision for a formula whereby due allowance will be made in the future for the rising cost of living, providing that it continues.
My friend the hon. member for Essex East put those words on Hansard the other day. I have cited those remarks made in three different speeches during the campaign and again over the air in order to show that there was a formal and definite representation to the senior citizens of Canada and indeed to the electors generally that when old age security legislation was introduced in September, as the Prime Minister said, that legislation would embody a provision or a formula by which the amount of pension would be tied in with changes in the cost of living. But notwithstanding that pledge, nowhere in the resolution now before the committee do we see any words that suggest that this is going to be embodied in the legislation. Indeed, I am extremely doubtful, Mr. Chairman, whether, having regard to the language of the legislation, it would now be competent for the government, on the present resolution, to introduce into the bill the very thing that the Prime Minister promised during his campaign, that is to say a formula whereby due allowance would be made in the future for the rise in the cost of living.
Though the minister may think that the government is fully implementing the Conservative pledges given to the senior citizens

Old Age Security Act
of Canada during the campaign, I want to point out that the proposed resolution does not carry out what the Prime Minister promised in this respect. I do not address any personal reproach to him for that fact because, having had the opportunity of going over the newspaper accounts of the Prime Minister's speeches during the campaign, I do not believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare could be expected to have taken account of all the promises that were made because there have been so many of them, and he could not be expected to have a record of all of them. However, I want to emphasize the fact that this was a promise, not made casually but one that was made three times during the campaign at meetings and was repeated again over the radio.
Then there was the third point, namely that the pensions were to be geared to national productivity. I can readily understand how enthusiastic the audience in Toronto would be on hearing that the pension was going to be geared to national productivity which, I suppose, would mean the gross national product. But nowhere in the resolution do we find anything about that matter either. The point I want to emphasize is this. In reading what was said the other day during the course of the discussion of this resolution I noted that one of the government members suggested, "But give us time". Mr. Chairman, this is the sort of thing that should be done now.
The lawyers are perfectly capable of drafting a formula about which the Prime Minister spoke in Toronto. They are perfectly capable of drafting some kind of clause which would, as the Prime Minister suggested in Toronto, gear the amount of the pension to national productivity. But nowhere in the resolution do we find anything either about the cost of living or about national productivity. Consequently, I hope that in these circumstances I may be permitted to differ with the Minister of National Health and Welfare in his assessment of the extent to which the government is carrying out the promises that were made in such explicit terms during the election campaign.
I should also like to remind the minister of another pledge the Prime Minister made, namely that a Conservative government would establish a commission to investigate fully the United States social security program. Let me quote from the account published by the Globe and Mail on May 1 of the Prime Minister's meeting at Antigonish in Nova Scotia. Here is what the account says:
Opening the Nova Scotia phase of his campaign in the agricultural community of Antigonish this

afternoon, Mr. Diefenbaker promised that a Conservative government would establish a commission to investigate fully the U.S. social security program. For only slightly increased costs, Mr. Diefenbaker said, the U.S. is able to pay its elderly and retired citizens far greater benefits than the $46 a month received by Canada's old age pensioners.
Mr. Chairman, the minister will have a further opportunity of speaking and I hope that he will tell us then what steps are being taken to implement that pledge of the Prime Minister in connection with old age security.
There is another aspect of this whole question on which I would like to touch and that is the question of cost. The minister has told us that it is estimated that the additional cost resulting from the legislation to be based on this resolution would be about $96 million in the first full year. As I understood him the other day he said that the increase in the amount of the pension itself accounts for $92 million.

As I say, we start off with this figure of $1,050 million and therefore to determine what are to be the costs of the national program with the proposed additions we must add the increase resulting from the larger number of persons who in this present year will be in receipt of benefits. My estimate of the amount of that increase, after looking at the available figures, is that it will come to probably $30 million. Mr. Chairman, just before the committee rose at six o'clock I had pointed out that if one were to try to calculate the
Old Age Security Act
estimated cost of the program of health, welfare and social security on the basis of a full year the method of calculation would be to start with last year's total of $1,050 million, add to it the increase of $30 million resulting from there being a larger number of persons in receipt of benefits, the $108 million which was voted earlier in this year 1957 and the approximate additional cost of the new measures; that is to say, the additional payments under old age security and the accessory measures, another $106 million. I also pointed out that in round figures the total of those different elements came in round figures to some $1,300 million annually.
I would like to emphasize that of course this does not include amounts paid in allowances to veterans or other expenditures in connection with veterans that come under another classification in the government's expenditures. I want to point out that this total amount of approximately $1,300 million is a very substantial sum of money and to go on to add that it is in fact more than one-quarter of all the taxes paid into the consolidated revenue fund and into the old age security fund, and considerably more that a quarter of the tax revenues that remain available to the federal government after it has turned over to the provinces the amounts to which they are entitled under the taxsharing agreements.
Of course, many of the hon. members who are now on the government benches and who have been in opposition will realize the difficulty for someone in opposition to make a precise calculation, but from the figures which are available it is possible to say that of every tax dollar retained by the federal treasury more than 27 cents are required to meet the cost of health, welfare and social security.
In considering the aggregate cost of $1,300 million which I mentioned a moment ago we must not overlook the commitments of the federal government in connection with the national scheme of hospitalization insurance which, when in force in all the provinces, will add a further amount of approximately $200 million annually to the cost of health, welfare and social security which are borne by the federal government. Of course, Mr. Chairman, as you will realize there are other costs which are borne by the provincial governments but I am considering at the moment only those which are payable out of the tax dollar which the federal government itself retains after it has handed back to the provinces the amounts to which they are entitled under the tax sharing agreements.
I wish to emphasize that we in the opposition, despite our familiarity with affairs that existed in the earlier part of this year, no

Old Age Security Act
longer have available to us information as to the expenditures which are to be incurred in the current year nor those to be undertaken next year; nor have we any information as to the probable revenues either for this year or for the fiscal year to begin on April 1 next. I mention that date, of course, because we all fully appreciate that the full burden of the increases which have already been made this year and those which are now under consideration will only be felt in the fiscal year 1958-59. In consequence of the situation I have just outlined it is not possible to come to a final judgment as to whether the additional expenditures which the present measure contemplates will fit into the general framework of a balanced budget.
I recall, as other hon. members do, some of the promises made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign. He said that a Progressive Conservative government would carry out its declared policy of increasing old age pensions and of reducing taxes. If I interpret correctly the words he used at Saskatoon he indicated that the costs of implementing these proposals-that of increasing old age pensions and reducing taxes- would be about $300 million. For old age security, old age assistance, allowances to the blind and to the disabled, we are at the moment, so to speak, using up $100 million, so it may be reasonable to expect that the government will make reductions in taxes amounting to some $200 million.
Our difficulties in the matter, Mr. Chairman, are not diminished by the fact that we do not know from the estimates which the Minister of Finance has tabled exactly what expenditures the government proposes to make and, therefore, though I have given much time to the task I have been unable to form any precise estimate of the over-all effect the government's measures are likely to have on the balance of the budget. In the circumstances it seems to me that the responsibility for establishing social security payments at these new levels must rest fairly and squarely on the shoulders of the government and I hope when the Minister of National Health and Welfare speaks later in this debate he will give us a clear statement as to the effect on the national budget of the higher level of the social security payments.
Like Canadians generally I welcome these further advances in the social security program. I think all Canadians welcome advances that can both be sustained and supported by the Canadian people but I hope the government is not proposing to maintain budget equilibrium by reducing expenditures for national defence because I believe that

Canadians generally would be gravely disquieted if advances in social security were to be made at the expense of national security.
Before closing my remarks I would like to refer very briefly to the comments of the Minister of Public Works. I thought it was unfortunate that he seemed to feel it necessary to speak about the Prime Minister's personal qualities. So far as I know they have not been in dispute at any time before this committee. We have known him for a>
long time and during the course of this discussion I do not think the good qualities of the Prime Minister were in dispute at any time. However, the remarks of the Minister of Public Works have been made and I think therefore I should say that having enjoyed the friendship of the hon. member for Essex East for a great many years, both before he became minister of national health and welfare and while he occupied that important office, I know that his interest in the little people of Canada was not surpassed by that of any other hon. member of this house.

Mr. Chairman, before making the remarks I intend to make I should like to offer my congratulations to the new Minister of National Health and Welfare on the great honour that has been bestowed upon him. I must say that when I first heard of his appointment I thought, "What? Another Ontario member appointed to the cabinet?". However, upon further consideration I realized that we in this group have always felt that His Excellency's advisers ought to be the most able men in the government regardless of where in Canada they happen to live and therefore we have no difficulty in congratulating him on his appointment. I am sure that if the new minister will show the same feeling of devotion for the cause of public health and human welfare as was shown by his late colleague, Doctor Blair, he will be serving the people of Canada right well.
This resolution is a vindication of some remarks I made when I was asked to comment on the election results and when I expressed the opinion that almost regardless of what legislation would be forthcoming, the people

Of Canada would not fail to reap some of the benefits of the upset that had taken place.
>
I, along with my colleagues, welcome this resolution. We welcome the increase that is being proposed from $46 a month to $55 a month. We welcome most sincerely the reduction in residential requirements from 20 years to 10 years. This was a promise made by the Secretary of State in the election campaign and I am very pleased indeed to see that the lady member of the cabinet is exercising her influence and that at least her promise in the campaign is being fulfilled.
I regret that in the resolution the government has not seen fit to give notice that the age is to be lowered from 70 to 65 for purposes of the Old Age Security Act. In these Rays when it is becoming increasingly difficult for our older citizens to find employment I feel that it would have been in the national interest had the government seen fit to lower the age requirement. Incidentally, it would also have saved a lot of money for the provincial authorities across Canada.
I read with some interest the remarks made the other day by the hon. member for Mackenzie River, who referred to the government members as being monkeys, as reported at page 430 of Hansard. Well that may be so in his opinion. However, when I listen to Liberal participants in this debate I really wonder who the monkeys are because it seems rather illogical that only a few months ago they asked us to be responsible members of parliament. They claimed that the economy of our country was able to afford only $46 a month. Now they are chastising the new Prime Minister for not making the old age pension even higher. Even the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount felt that the Prime Minister was not adhering to his promises and this was not a sufficient amount to meet the rising cost of living and to provide an adequate standard of living for those people. I find the Liberal predicament most amusing indeed. They are already chastising this government for failure to keep its promises; yet the Canadian people will not easily forget that for 38 years the Liberals have promised a national health insurance plan and we have not it yet. Therefore I feel when we begin to compare election promises we at this time are a little hasty if we complain overly much about any failures which might exist in that respect.
I will agree also that within the present framework of monetary and fiscal policies the $55 may possibly be about as far as this government is able to go. This government is unwilling to adopt a new approach to the role and function of government in our economic life. They also, like the former government, prefer to let a few individuals not
Old Age Security Act
responsible to the people manage the economy of the nation and therefore within that framework maybe $55 a month is about what we ought to have expected of the government. As my colleague, the hon. member for Regina City, pointed out the other day, and as was emphasized by a number of other colleagues, we feel that our economy is well able to provide at least $75 a month to all of our people at age 65.
The hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount pointed out at some length the expenses involved at the present time on the part of the federal government on behalf of public welfare and social security measures.
I accepted his figures and I did some rather rapid calculation. To him it was becoming a rather serious matter that we were spending four per cent of our gross national production in providing our Canadian people with social security and health measures. To me it does not seem to be a level that is anywhere near the danger point and we in this section feel that a much larger percentage might very well be provided to the most important causes of public health and social security.
When we look at this resolution, Mr. Chairman, we note that it deals only with the amount of the pension that is received by the old age pensioner at the end of his life. I feel that there are other matters that might have been included in this resolution and possibly in other resolutions which are of equal importance to our senior citizens. I look at some of the representations that have been made on this subject by organizations of our senior citizens and I notice that all of them without fail do not ask only for an increase in the old age pension, they all ask for a number of other considerations. I note that first and foremost they place heavy emphasis on health care.
To an old age pensioner an assurance that in his declining years his health, his medical and hospital needs will be met is, I submit, of far greater importance than adding a few dollars to his monthly income. I have spoken to various meetings of aid age pensioners and those meetings invariably agreed that if some measures were undertaken in the field of relieving them of this constant worry they would greatly appreciate it. They are very keenly aware of the fact that sooner or later -and for most of them sooner-they will be needing medical care, they will be needing hospital care and some consideration along those lines is of more importance to them than adding to the amount of the old age pension cheques at the end of the month.

Old Age Security Act
Then I noticed another thing they feel very keenly on, namely that they be supplied with low-cost housing. The other day the hon. member for Nanaimo pointed out exactly what is happening. Since arriving in Ottawa I have had numerous letters to that effect. There is fear and trembling among many of those who live in rented quarters, and most old age pensioners do, as to how much of the $9 increase the landlord is going to grab from them when their incomes are increased by that amount. Therefore I feel that low cost housing for our senior citizens is another way in which they can be helped, a way that might be equally important as an increase in their monthly income.
When the former Liberal government raised their pensions by $6 a month many hundreds of these people in the lower mainland of British Columbia had their rents raised by $5 a month and all that the senior citizen received out of the $6 was $1. I say that the government is doing the exact opposite of what I am now advocating. Under the National Housing Act there are various schemes whereby low rent housing might be supplied for our old age pensioners, but rather than making it easier for more of such housing to be built the-government has seen fit to raise the interest rate by another one-half of one per cent on houses built under section 16 of the National Housing Act.
I have always taken some measure of pride in what the government of British Columbia is doing in this respect, action begun by the former coalition government and now continued by the new regime. When low cost housing is built for senior citizens and others with similar low incomes the provincial government pays a grant of one-third of the cost of the building. All that the federal government does is to supply a mortgage on which they collect interest and the interest rate, as I indicated, is now 4j per cent. In my opinion, if the federal government would match the outright grant made by the provincial government it would go a long way toward reducing the rents that the senior citizens have to pay and making more housing available for them.
I sometimes feel rather keenly when I see young married men, many of whom are earning $400, $500 or $600 a month, living in new $12,000, $15,000 or $18,000 homes which have been built under the National Housing Act with government guaranteed money while our senior citizens who need government assistance have to continue living in musty basements and hot attic rooms in our urban areas.
[Mr. Regier.l
The argument of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on the resolution failed to impress me at all. He seemed rather to regret that the government was now going to pay the sum of $55 a month to our senior citizens. In his opinion some of the fishermen in Bonavista-Twillingate were earning less than that. That argument fails to convince. Such an argument is based on the philosophy of tearing everyone down to the level of the lowest, a philosophy to which I have never subscribed. It is the same as saying that we will not allow another immigrant into this country until every Canadian has a home and employment. It is the same argument as saying that we will never pay anyone an income of $5,000 a year until everyone has an income of $5,000 a year. I feel that argument is a rather vicious appeal to the voters of Bonavista-Twillingate. After all, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was an executive member of a government for many years and if these fishermen had such a measly income as he indicated he has no one else to blame but himself and his former colleagues.
I close my remarks by saying that I feel that the people of Canada, as evidenced by this resolution, are obtaining some of the benefits of a new government. At this time I should like to express the opinion that if the government had not been elected as a minority government this resolution would not now be on the order paper.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to make extended remarks on the resolution now before us. I am sure that the proposal, to grant additional assistance to our senior citizens, as well as those in other categories covered by other resolutions, will meet with the approval of the people of Canada as a whole. While so many of us are enjoying a good measure of the material things of life we cannot afford to neglect those who have not only laid the foundations of this great nation but have brought it to the high degree of prosperity and greatness that it has achieved.

Many of these people find themselves in the position where they are unable to gain for themselves the necessities of life and are unable to engage in remunerative employment. They are looking to us to see to it that they have sufficient in order to enable them to live and to spend the rest of their days in at least some measure of comfort and security.
Some of those who have participated in the debate have gone to considerable lengths to try to prove who should receive the credit for the inauguration of our social welfare program, especially with respect to old age pensions. I do not think that this is of too great importance. In my opinion the main consideration before us is this: Are we doing our utmost as a nation to see to it that those who are looking to us for assistance receive that assistance in a way that will not only discharge our moral obligation to them but will also indicate in some measure our appreciation for all they have done.
Some question has been raised as to whether or not the amendments now before us encompass in their totality the promises that were made by the Conservative party during the past few months. Be that as it may, I am of the opinion that their response to the challenge of the pressing need of our senior citizens has been much more commendable than was the response of the previous administration. Someone used the term "too little and too late". I think possibly that was true, because it was too little and too late to stave off the retribution that the Liberal party saw in the offing, and of course that was indicated very clearly in the events of June 10.
My Liberal opponent in the Fraser valley, a splendid young man for whom I have a great deal of respect, found himself hard pressed to justify the stand of the Liberal government with respect to old age pensions, especially in relation to the $6 raise. On one occasion he made the observation that if the pension were raised too high it would rob the children of the privilege and responsibility of contributing to the support of their parents in their old age. He was never able to adequately answer the question that was asked, under a set-up like that what are the old maids and bachelors going to do?
In any event, we are faced today with these particular amendments. The first is to increase the amount of the monthly pension to those eligible under the terms of the Old Age Security Act to $55; second, to reduce the basic residence requirement from 20 to 10 years; third, to increase the length
Old Age Security Act
of permissible temporary absence of pensioners from Canada from three to six months. I believe that these proposed amendments cover, in part, three of the main objections which have been raised in the past relative to the old age security legislation. I say "in part" because although improving conditions to an appreciable degree additional amendments will be required to bring this legislation more closely into line with reality.
First of all, with respect to the increase in the monthly pension to $55, I may say that I do not believe there is any question in the minds of the members of this house or in the minds of the people across Canada relative to the need for an increase in this allowance. I believe ordinary common sense would indicate that it is absolutely impossible at the present time for senior citizens to live in any degree of comfort on $46 a month. I know the suggestion has been made that this pension was never intended to be their sole income; it was to supplement their savings, what they are allowed to have, or it was just to provide a little extra for them. I think we must remember that many of these people were so busy building this nation of ours, making the sacrifices that were necessary, they did not have any time to make provision for the closing years of their lives. Now they are faced with trying to live on $46 a month. I am sure that none of us would try to infer that that was adequate under the present circumstances.
I am not going to attempt to review the great mass of written material that has been placed on the records across this country presenting the needs of the senior citizens. I think that would be superfluous. I believe that each one of us has observed for himself the conditions in which many of our senior citizens are living or existing, and because of our personal observations we are convinced that an increase is absolutely essential. I do not think there is any question as to the urgency of the proposal. For too long our senior citizens have been forced to live below the borderline of poverty. We must act, and we should act quickly to bring them some assistance that will help them in time of need.
Regarding the amount that has been proposed by this resolution, I wonder if it is the best we can do in the light of our ability as a nation to pay? I was listening, as other members were, to the observations made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. He put on the record once again his own personal conviction, and the conviction of others

Old Age Security Act
of his group, that Canada is well able to pay $75 a month to our senior citizens at the age of 65.

He-

-admitted if his party had come to power it would not have increased pensions to the $75 a month it had advocated in the last campaign, but likely would have made them $60 or $65 a month because of the need to introduce other social legislation.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that newspapers do not always get the facts absolutely straight. Hon. members have pointed out on different occasions that they have been misquoted. If this is a wrong statement then I would be very happy if the leader of the C.C.F. party would make the necessary correction right at the moment, but that is as I have read it from this article taken from this morning's newspaper.
The question is, as I say, is this amount of $55 in keeping with Canada's ability to pay? We think of the continuing rise in the cost of living and, as has been pointed out, the tendency on the part of some landlords to increase rents. This may be justifiable when we look at the situation squarely because it may be that some of these landlords had been providing rooms for pensioners at a very low rate and at some sacrifice to themselves. I do not know, but that may be so. Nevertheless, our pensioners are faced with continually increasing costs of living and an increase in rents as well.
The second part of this resolution proposes to make a reduction in the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years. I believe that this proposal is commendable. There are those who would propose that the residence qualification should be removed altogether. Personally I am of the opinion that there is some justification for the continuation of that principle. However, I do agree that the 10-year period is much more just than the 20-year period that is presently in effect.
