Earlier speakers have covered rather fully the history of the old age pension in Canada, but I want to touch on two main points, first of all the relationship of the government old age security measures to other pension measures in Canada, such as civil service pensions, company pensions and the savings of ordinary individual Canadians and, secondly, the matter touched on by my friend the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount, the financing of this very large expenditure.
I think we should recall that pensions were originally a field of provincial responsibility. In 1926 when the first old age pension system

Old Age Security Act
started it was made a matter of joint federal-provincial responsibility. The provinces did not turn over all authority to the federal government as they did when the amendment with respect to unemployment insurance came into effect. The first payments in 1926 were, of course, $20 on a means test, paid half by the federal government and half by the provinces which was an indication of their awareness of their responsibility. We British Columbians are proud that our province was the first province to pass the necessary supplemental legislation and the first province to actually pay an old age pension at Alberni in 1926. At that time, we remember, the means test was justified on the reasoning that this was a matter of giving to those in need money available from the treasury to assist them in meeting the cost of living. The total cost that first year was $12 million which was a large sum for the budget of Canada at that time.
Over the years the sum increased from $20 to $40. The federal government raised its share to three-quarters of the total cost and the three western provinces accepted further responsibility in this joint field by paying additional supplements on another means test ranging all the way up to the $20 now paid in British Columbia.
As time went on the feeling developed that the means test was unfair, that there was something mean about it. It came to be thought of as bearing a stigma of charity and we all know of many elderly people who needed this assistance but refused to apply for it because they were too proud. Their attitude was that they were not going to accept charity from the government. Above all, it was regarded as unfair because it denied assistance to those Canadians who had tried to plan for their own retirement by joining company pension schemes, by buying annuities or by their personal savings and investments.
It was because of that we had an exhaustive study made of the question by a parliamentary committee in 1950 and 1951 and as a consequence the new legislation came into being which paid $40 to every Canadian who had 20 years residence in Canada at age 70. That was paid entirely by the federal government, and $40 to those in need at age 65, paid on a means test, the cost shared jointly by the federal and provincial governments.
While the earlier pensions were paid entirely out of general revenue, for the first time in that year we gave to this pension scheme a contributory aspect by levying an extra tax of 2 per cent on personal income with a ceiling of $60, by levying 2 per cent extra by way of tax on corporation profits and by levying an extra 2 per cent in the form of a general sales tax.

We remember how gladly these changes were received at the time. They removed the stigma of charity since every one received the pension at age 70. It was a real supplement to the savings of those people who had tried to provide for their own old age.
Over the years, of course, the government had urged people not to depend on the government in their old age and encouraged people to make provision for their retirement. I think the first action of this kind was the sale of government annuities, the government undertaking the cost of administration, and then followed the drives to sell government savings bonds. Encouragement was given to company pension schemes by making the contributions of both the employees and the employers tax deductible. Today the vast majority of company employees in Canada have this safeguard of contributing to company pension plans through which they and their employers are making provision for their own old age.
Last spring the former government extended this aid to the last great group not covered in the country, the self-employed, by allowing them to deduct before tax 10 per cent of income up to a maximum ceiling of $2,500 a year which they could invest in their own retirement plans.
All these things are admirable, of course, but we in this house are all aware of what has happened to the savings of individuals in recent years because of the continuous inflationary trends in the world. Pensions which were regarded as adequate when these people planned for their retirement are now proving pitifully inadequate because of the loss in purchasing power of the dollar.
It is for that reason, of course, we hear in this house pleas for increases in the pensions of retired civil servants, whose small salaries and pensions seemed adequate at the time but whose pensions are proving inadequate today. The government in the past resisted giving special treatment to the civil servants on the grounds that if it helped these civil servants in retirement then it should help every other Canadian in retirement, retired people other than civil servants whose savings were no longer adequate because of inflation.
It was in 1952 that the first real measure of assistance was given to this group by the introduction of the old age security at 70, free from the means test, because then those people with their own savings got the added government pension of $40 a month. It gave, of course, no help to people in this group between the age of 65 and 69 who, because of their own savings, were denied assistance under the means test.

The last government also in 1957 increased the basic pension from $40 to $46 a month, increasing the cost of the old age pension to taxpayers of Canada from $400 million a year to $460 million a year. T do not intend to fight the election over again but we all remember the Conservatives said this was inadequate, the 15 per cent increase was inadequate. They were not specific in the amount they promised. The Social Credit promised $100 a month and the C.C.F. $75 a month. Well, out west, and in British Columbia, too, we still remember the promises of the Social Credit away back in 1935 to pay $25 a month to every citizen. Therefore, the promise of $100 a month was just four times as phony as that promise. So far as the C.C.F. are concerned, their promise of $75 a month in this field of joint responsibility is in contrast with the actual record of performance of the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan in this field of joint responsibility. Last year they paid to the senior citizens $550,000, a little more than half a million dollars, in contrast with the $23 million a year paid out by the federal treasury.
The $6 increase cost the taxpayers of Canada an extra $60 million a year but, of course, this was never mentioned by opposition speakers in the last campaign. They broke it down the other way, $6, 20 cents a day. The other day the hon. member for York West called it two cups of coffee a day. I am waiting until he stands up and describes this $9 increase of the Tories as three cups Of coffee a day. I do not intend to get into an argument like that except to say that the old age pensioners in Canada were glad of the $6 and they are glad of the $9.
One of the questions, however, which arises out of this is the feeling of the Canadian people that this $6 was inadequate, despite the fact that it was a 15 per cent increase over the previous pension and despite the fact that the cost of living, since this pension was brought in in 1952, had not increased 15 per cent. I think the answer is quite clear. The $6 may have made up the loss in purchasing power since 1952 of the old age security pension of $40, but it did not make up the loss of purchasing power in the same period of the private savings of our senior citizens, the savings which most Canadians do intend to carry them through their own old age; that is, their total retirement income composed of the old age pension paid at 70 plus their company pension plan or their government annuities or their own personal savings.
We have heard the promise of the Prime Minister in this regard. As far as the cost of
Old Age Security Act
living bonus on the old age pension is concerned I suggest that to be effective it has got to be more than a cost of living bonus on the old age pension. I hope that when this bill comes forward after the resolution is adopted it will contain a provision for an automatic annual revision based on the year-end cost of living to maintain the purchasing power, not just of the old age pension but of a minimum basic retirement income. A very modest basic retirement income would be $200 a month for a couple on old age security, made up of $110 a month from the new $55 pension, plus $90 of their own savings or pensions.
Many Canadians of course have more than $90 a month for their own retirement; some have less. But this $200 a month retirement income would be a very modest start. An annual adjustment could be made each year on the cost of living at December. The present inflationary trend in North America is about three per cent a year. That would be an extra $6 on this basic retirement income of $200. That would be $6 a month, $3 on each of the old age pensions paid to this couple and that would maintain the purchasing power of their retirement income composed of the old age security pension paid by the federal government and their own savings. If, of course, the government is able to hold the line on inflation there would be no increase in the cost of living and no need for any increase.
I think such a provision would have immediate and very salutary effects. It would assure all Canadians now trying to provide for their own old age through personal savings, company pension plans or annuities, that they in the future would have at least $200 a month in constant purchasing power, provided that they had an income themselves of $90 a month on retirement. It would relieve them of a great deal of worry; it would also relieve young people today who are trying to plan for their own old age of worry and of their attempts now to hedge against inflation by dabbling in common stocks and real estate as well. Those who have been dabbling in common stocks, of course, have been shocked in the last year by the decline in the stock market, adding to their bewilderment when they try effectively to provide for their own old age. It would also remove the future problems of retired civil servants on low pension who are asking for increases in their pensions because of the decline in purchasing power. Above all, it would remove the old age pension from the political arena and save us all from the spectacle of political parties trying to bribe the electors with their own money with election promises of higher

Old Age Security Act
and higher pensions, the height of the promises being directly related to the unlikelihood of the party succeeding to office.
I think the other aspect of this pension which must command attention now is the matter of paying for them. I firmly believe that all these social security benefits, paid for out of the government treasury, should have a price tag on them so that the taxpayers whose money is being used will have some idea of the cost and the benefits. This is an extremely important thing because there are taxpayers, citizens as well, in this country who have the deluded belief that these social security benefits fall like manna from heaven, from this remote government at Ottawa.
I think a good start was made in the 1952 bill by the 2 per cent, 2 per cent, 2 per cent formula, increases in the personal income tax, the corporation tax and the sales tax. We have not, of course, the direct contribution that the United States social security plan has but this was a good step forward. In practice, however, I doubt whether many Canadian wage earners are very conscious of these extra taxes. They are not conscious of the two per cent extra sales tax because that is paid at the manufacturer's level.
The average Canadian is not conscious of the extra 2 per cent corporation tax, although he pays it in the end, because that is buried in the accounts of the big corporations when they are prepared by their accountants at the end of the year. He is aware of the 2 per cent on the income tax just once a year when he makes out his own income tax return. These three 2 per cent taxes did not quite pay the cost of the $40 a month pension. I notice the most recent figures-that is, on the $46 a month pension-indicate that the fund is running behind over $10 million a month. With the $96 million increase which the minister has announced for the new increase, the fund is going to be running *behind something around $215 million a year. In other words, about two-thirds will be met by the taxes and one-third apparently is going to come out of the central treasury.
I think there are two reasons why this should not be done. One of the criticisms levied most often by the C.C.F. speakers against the present old age security pension is that millionaires get it, a reversal of the old argument that the previous pension was demeaned because it was given on a means test.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a very few minutes of the time of the committee to comment on the resolution now before us. I was very much interested in listening to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano review the history of old age pensions and other social security benefits in

Canada, particularly his attempt to get the house to believe that every advance that has been made was due to the high spirit and the big heart of the Liberal party. Of course, there were some things in that history that he conveniently left out, and I hope in the course of the few minutes that I take to fill in certain details that he significantly left out.
It is all very well, of course, for the hon. member to indicate to us that the Liberal party was the great benefactor of the Canadian people all the way through the years since old age pensions were first paid, but I remind him and the members of his party that as late as 1936 and 1937 they were still holding the old age pension to a limit of $20 a month. Part of that was to be paid by the provincial governments and part by the municipal governments, with the federal government paying 75 per cent.
When the Social Credit government first came into office in Alberta in 1935 I recall that we began urging the Liberal government at Ottawa to increase the old age pension. In every session of the legislature that I attended beginning in 1935 until well after 1940 I recall that we passed resolutions calling upon the federal government to introduce a higher level of pension. These were sent regularly to the federal government and on one or two occasions I came to Ottawa with delegations to sit in with the minister of finance and other federal government ministers to see what could be done about improving administration in the old age pension field. I recall very definitely on each occasion putting a case to the federal government at Ottawa for higher pensions.
Nothing whatever was done until much later than 1937, but the province of Alberta, realizing that the federal Liberal government would do nothing, began in 1938 to pay a supplementary allowance of $5 a month over and above what the federal government was prepared to share, and we paid it without a means test. We continued to pay it to our aged citizens without a means test for some years. Shortly after 1940 the province of Alberta increased the supplementary payment to $10 a month without a means test and only then did the Liberal government at Ottawa, feeling much embarrassed and much ashamed of their attitude, decide to come in and try to do something a little better than the miserable $20 they had hung on to for so many years. They were actually shamed into doing it by the fact that the government of my province paid a supplementary allowance of $10 a month for some years with no assistance from the federal government or no sharing of the amount by that government.
Old Age Security Act

I shall be happy to comply with your request. I should like for just a minute, now that I have replied to my hon. friend who is so glib in this house when he has no responsibility, but when he had was not so ready to come to grips with things, to say just a word about something that has not been mentioned as yet in connection with this resolution. I think we have stressed adequately, from our group at least, our feelings with regard to the necessity for taking care of our aged citizens. I believe that the status of a nation can be judged pretty well

by the way they treat their senior citizens; that has been so for a great many years. I am very happy to see the basic pension raised to $55 per month. In Alberta we are going to continue to pay the supplementary allowance, which will bring the pension to $70 per month. This $70 comes somewhere near to an adequate pension under the circumstances; not too high by any means, but at least it is getting into that realm.
There is a point that I think ought to be stressed, and that is in connection with the economic effects. Over the years it has been contended by people that we might get ourselves into economic difficulties by increasing the old age pension to a point where there was a reasonable living allowance granted. I do not believe that. As long as this country can produce from $30 billion to $32 billion worth of goods and services a year there is no reason whatever why the aged citizens of this country should not have a standard of living that is comparable to that which is granted to other citizens or made available to other citizens.
I do not mean to say that the government should be prepared to give our aged citizens as much as other people can earn, but certainly there is no reason why there should not be an escalator clause attached to the qualifications for the old age pension, so that when the cost of living goes up the pension rises in proportion. These people are considered to be on a fixed income, but they are not. Really they are on a declining income because the purchasing power of the dollar is continuously declining. These people who are considered to be on a fixed income ought to have an escalator clause attached to the qualification for their pension.
It seems to me if we had something of that kind we would be doing nothing more than is right and fair. Did you ever consider, Mr. Chairman, what happens when we pay old age pensions to people? Old age pensions are the very best source, are the very best type, put it that way, of new purchasing power. The pension is spent almost immediately. Did you ever consider that whenever we pay a pension to our aged citizens they do not run off to Timbuctoo to spend their money. They spend it at the corner grocery in the community where they live. They are the best supporters of the small merchants, the little businessman. They spend their money immediately they receive it for the things which this country produces. As they do that they are helping to stabilize the economic affairs of this country; stabilizing business, stabilizing production and prices. Certainly, they are not contributing in any way to uncontrollable inflation.

If reasonable precaution is taken there is no reason why a $75 per month pension should be inflationary in a country that is increasing as this country is in its productive capacity year by year. I would say that where it is necessary to introduce new purchasing power for consumer goods in order to attempt to stabilize the economy, the old age pensioners are the very best source of spending power. To give them new purchasing power does help to stabilize our economy better than any other way of which I know. For that reason, if for no other reason, I support the proposed increase to $55 per month which this government has brought before us today.
I feel that enough has been said about the matter of residence qualifications. I do not intend to raise that again. I know that there are some in the country, particularly members of labour unions, who are just a bit concerned about reducing the residence qualifications from 20 to 10 years. I have not been convinced that their fears are well founded as yet. I do know quite well a number of aged citizens who came to this country and contributed the very best they had over a period of years, then found themselves about age 70 or over with nothing to take care of them in their declining years. I feel it is only right and just that something be granted to them, even though they have not been here for 20 years. Whether or not 10 years is the best place to cut off, I do not know, but I am prepared to support it until I am shown a better way.
So far as the other proposal is concerned, that is the period of allowable absence from the country, I am prepared to go along with that too until we have something better shown to us.

Mr. Chairman, I may be guilty of a certain degree of naivete because I have the feeling that the wording of this motion is that it is expedient to introduce a measure to do certain things. I have heard a great deal of discussion here tonight but very little of it has been on the basis of the necessity for introducing this particular bill. So far as I am concerned, I think the word "expedient" which means advantageous or suitable is an extremely pallid and totally inadequate word to express necessity for bringing in this particular bill.
For many years now it has been quite obvious that the senior citizens of this country have been in a serious position having regard to their ability to meet their needs. I think that in bringing in this legislation the word "imperative" would have been a much more expressive word to use than is the word "expedient" because it has been and is

extremely imperative that this belated assistance to our senior citizens be brought forward. I note that, on the basis of the 1949 consumers price index, the cost of living stands today at 123.3. That is the latest figure for September.
That is 23 per cent higher than it was in 1950 when the pension was brought in and I would point out that since the cost of living has risen to that extent it is absolutely necessary that our older citizens be given a reasonable chance to meet the rising cost of living. So far no adequate attempt has been made to meet that necessity. Our friends on the other side of the house brought in what they choose to call a 15 per cent raise last year; that 15 per cent raise was to meet the rising cost of living which was at that time slightly over 20 per cent. How they proposed to meet a 20 per cent rise in the cost of living with a 15 per cent rise in the pension is entirely beyond my comprehension.
The unfortunate thing about the consumers' price index is that it deals merely with those things which are absolutely essential for the well-being of the senior citizens of this country and so far as I am concerned I believe it is necessary that these people be given a chance to enjoy a reasonable degree of happiness and pleasure such as is enjoyed by we who today have a higher standard of living. Unless their income is such that they are going to be able to enjoy life in this way we are not dealing with them in the way we should be and it is up to this government, since they have assumed responsibility for the welfare of these people, to provide them not only with the necessities of life but to make other adequate provision for these people.
When you look at the consumers' price index you find it includes such items as food, shelter, clothing and household operations. Under the heading of household operations are included fuel, electricity, home furnishings, supplies and services. What the index does not tell you is that household operations have risen 19 per cent since 1949, that food has risen 21.9 per cent and that shelter has risen 36.4 per cent. These things are all absolutely necessary to the well-being of our senior citizens and we are just barely meeting these costs under the provisions of this bill. Therefore I would not like it to be thought for one moment, although I am going to go along with the bill, that I regard it as adequate, I do not.
The consumers' price index does not include the things which go toward making life pleasant and happy. Surely if anybody in this world and particularly in this Canada of

ours has earned the right to happiness and pleasure in life it is those people who have spent their days bringing this country from a state of wilderness to a wonderland. Yet we play around, as our government have done in the past, chiseling these people from their income. That is what we are doing when we allow the cost of living to rise in such a way that it cuts down the livelihood these people are getting to a point where they are on the verge of bare sustenance and no more.
This practice of cutting down and chiseling with respect to these inadequate incomes has been brought about simply because the governments of the past have not seen fit to introduce a monetary policy which would prevent fluctuations and make this kind of legislation entirely unnecessary.
I want to point out that for this reason I am in favour of bringing in this particular resolution and the proposed bill that will follow it, in addition to the bill to provide for advance payments for prairie grain which was passed this afternoon. I believe this particular government is slowly but surely beginning to see the light. I admit quite frankly that although it seems that vision is extremely dim at the present time, as time goes along that vision may grow.
They are beginning to recognize that the injection of purchasing power into the consumers' market is the soundest method of stabilizing our economy. It is the only method that will expand our economy without bringing about inflation. The time is coming when the government of this country must recognize the fact that there is only one reason for production, and that is consumption. We do not care where the consumers live; it does not make any difference whether they live in one of the small towns of our own country or in Timbuktu or Sumatra, it is the consumer that really matters and he holds the key to economic progress. As long as we can keep the consumer happy and see that he is able to consume the goods we produce we can be assured that our production capacity will more than keep pace with demand in any given period. I will close by saying that I would, like Thomas Jefferson, sooner dream of the future than pin my faith to the history of the past.
